headline: Kiwi Return to Wellington After 150 Years of Absence
meta_description: Over 250 kiwi birds have been successfully returned to Wellington's hills for the first time in 150 years through a community and iwi-led conservation effort.
summary_short: More than 250 kiwi have been translocated back to Wellington's hills for the first time in over a century, thanks to a partnership between iwi, landowners, and communiti…
body:
For the first time in 150 years, kiwi once again inhabit the hills surrounding Wellington, Aotearoa New Zealand. More than 250 of these iconic birds have been successfully translocated to the region through the Capital Kiwi Project, a collaboration between iwi (Māori nations), community members, and landowners. The effort represents far more than a simple species reintroduction—it is grounded in relationships, cultural responsibility, and the restoration of connection between people and land. Project lead Paul Ward emphasizes that success depends on three essential relationships: with iwi, with communities, and with landowners. "If you pull one of those legs off, the tripod falls over," he says.

The practical work was substantial. Teams deployed over 5,300 traps across approximately 24,000 hectares to remove stoats, invasive predators that hunt young kiwi before they reach "fighting weight"—one kilogram, when they can defend themselves. Yet removing predators was only the beginning. The project required years of relationship-building, bird translocation, and community education, particularly for Wellington residents who had never seen a kiwi in person.

Crucially, the transfer of birds followed Māori protocol. Kiwi are gifted to the project through a tono (a traditional gifting process) and then welcomed to communities through a pōwhiri (a Māori welcoming ceremony). Rāwiri Walsh, the project's Kaimanaaki Kiwi (kiwi guardian), explains that this approach ensures iwi authority and agreement at every stage. Including newly hatched chicks that survived to fighting weight, the project now sustains over 300 kiwi in Wellington's surrounding hills. Ward views this as a proof of concept for reintroducing other taonga (valued species) to the region, anchored not in scientific ambition alone, but in the shared belief that humans and land are inseparable.
quick_facts: Over 250 kiwi translocated to Wellington hills for first time in 150 years
5,300+ traps deployed across 24,000 hectares to remove invasive stoats
Kiwi gifted through tono and welcomed via pōwhiri, traditional Māori ceremonies
Over 300 kiwi now live in Wellington region, including newly hatched chicks
